findings.title: User-storage recovery codes are reusable and not ordered
findings.body: isValid deserializes the stored raw code list and returns true if any entry equals the submitted value, then leaves the list unchanged. Recovery codes are one-time and must be used in order: the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider hashes the input, matches only the next remaining code, and deletes it. credentialManager().isValid stops at the user-storage validator when that provider supports and is configured for the type, so the local provider never runs for credentials accepted by CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential. RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator does not consume the code after a successful check; it only re-reads the credential. The same backup code can be replayed forever, and a code other than the one the login form requested is accepted. The new test logs in only once, so it does not catch this.

findings.title: Recovery-code login form crashes unless storage returns Keycloak's internal model
findings.body: The bean loads a credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential and immediately calls Optional.get() and RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel. That parser requires credentialData and secretData in the hashed recovery-code schema and throws NoSuchElementException or RuntimeException otherwise. When user storage's updateCredential returns true, createRecoveryCodesCredential does not persist that model; it only sends a JSON array of raw codes on a UserCredentialModel. isConfiguredFor can still be true, so the authenticator renders this bean. A provider that stores the updateCredential payload and returns it, or that implements supportsCredentialType, updateCredential, isConfiguredFor, and isValid but not getCredentials, makes recovery-code login fail with a server error before a code can be submitted. There is no fallback to a local credential or a default index. Only the test storage papers over this by rebuilding a model in getCredentials.

findings.title: Exhausted user-storage recovery credentials are not deleted
findings.body: After a successful check, if the credential from RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential reports allCodesUsed(), the authenticator calls removeStoredCredentialById. That API deletes only credentials in Keycloak's database. Credentials stored because user storage updateCredential returned true are not there, and the test storage's getCredentials rebuild does not copy the id assigned in updateCredential, so the id is often null and the delete is a no-op. The configure-recovery-codes required action is still added, but required actions run after the browser flow. On the next login the recovery authenticator is still configured, RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean calls getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get() on an empty list, and rendering the challenge throws. That exception aborts the authenticator instead of skipping it, so the user can be locked out even when another factor is configured.

findings.title: Plaintext recovery codes are sent to user storage
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential JSON-encodes the raw generatedCodes list and puts that string in the UserCredentialModel passed to updateCredential. The RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel argument already contains only hashes. Local storage persists those hashes; this path gives the federation provider every unused code in cleartext and drops userLabel and generatedAt, so they cannot be stored either. BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage writes that string unchanged into credentialData and keeps it for later equality checks. A storage dump or credential-update log discloses all backup codes, which authenticate as the user. Verification only needs the existing hashRawCode/verifyRecoveryCodeInput helpers, so the hashed secret data should be what is handed off, and the reference provider should not keep reversible codes.

findings.title: getCredentials drops the stored id and renumbers codes
findings.body: updateCredential sets an id with KeycloakModelUtils.generateId, but getCredentials ignores that CredentialModel and returns a new one from RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues. That factory does not copy the stored id and assigns fresh indexes starting at 0 to whatever list it is given. The same method now sets an id on OTP credentials because listing and deletion need it; recovery codes are returned with a null id, so account-console delete and removeStoredCredentialById cannot target them. If used codes are removed from the stored list, the remainder is renumbered and the login page asks for code 0 instead of the next original number. The rebuilt view also cannot be written back: its credentialData is metadata JSON, not the raw list isValid reads.

findings.title: Recovery codes cannot be disabled in the new storage support
findings.body: disableCredentialType clears OTP and otherwise only logs that the type is unsupported. getDisableableCredentialTypesStream only reports OTP, so recovery-authn-codes is not advertised as disableable. Admin REST disableCredentialType and account-console removal therefore leave myUser.recoveryCodes set. isConfiguredFor stays true and isValid still accepts the codes, so an administrator cannot revoke recovery codes after this provider has stored them.

findings.title: New test never checks replay, next-code index, revocation, or local fallback
findings.body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only checks that setup writes no Keycloak DB credential, that the storage flag is set, and that the first displayed code logs in once. It never submits that code again, never asserts a later login asks for the next index, never disables or deletes the credential, and never covers a user storage that returns false from updateCredential so the helper must keep the local hashed credential. Those are the paths this change adds and the ones the new storage implementation gets wrong, so the suite stays green while replay and revocation are broken.
